I have farmed these 14 mu for 40 years, and I know every piece of this land like the back of my hand. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. My household has five people — my son works in the county town, so my wife and I do most of the farm work, though he comes back to help at wheat harvest and maize planting. I keep 10 mu in the wheat-maize rotation because that is our foundation; it puts food on the table and gives us straw for the animals. The wheat went into the ground last October, and now in early spring I need to top-dress it with urea and irrigate from my well when the weather warms. I use improved wheat seed — I have tried many varieties over the years and I know which ones handle the dry winds here. For the summer maize, I plant Denghai 605 hybrid seed straight into the wheat stubble without ploughing; I learned this from my neighbors ten years ago and it saves time and fuel while the yield stays good. The other 4 mu I put into cotton. Cotton is more work — I have to spray more times for bollworm and aphids, and it needs more potassium — but when the cotton price is decent it pays for my grandson's school expenses. I do not deep-plough anymore; the rotary tiller is good enough for my soil and I am not as strong as I was at thirty.
